true_concept: Slow move missing forcing pawn break

In every position a player made a passive or retreating move (Nd7, Nef3, Be2, e5, Nf6, Qd1, Nc3) that abandoned an attacking piece/outpost and missed a concrete forcing tactical shot, usually a check or sacrifice. The tagger's tags (Missed Overloading, Missed Attacking Check, Missed Prophylaxis, etc.) fire on scattered side-effects and none names the unifying passive-move-misses-tactic pattern. Every position shares the same mechanism: a pawn or piece move vacates the ONLY defender of a friendly pawn, leaving it en prise (often with a follow-up fork). The tagger's top tag 'Allowed Pawn Capture' only names the generic side-effect (a pawn can be taken) without capturing the specific 'removed the pawn's sole defender' concept. The ALT label 'Undefended Pawn After Moving Defender' names the true concept precisely.

Most top positions are captures (Qxf7+, Qxf5+, Bxd5, dxc6) that grab a pawn/piece but immediately lose the capturing piece—usually the queen—to a simple recapture. The 'Greedy Capture' tag names this core mistake directly, and 'Hung Queen'/'Hung Material' also fits the frequent queen losses. The ALT label 'Hanging Piece Blunder' is accurate but less specific than the greedy-capture cause captured here.

Most positions share a failure to grab undefended/winnable material (Rxa2, Nxe5, Qxg4, axb4 winning the bishop). Every position is a quiet, non-urgent pawn/king move (a6, a3, g3, h3, b5) played while facing an immediate forcing threat—either a missed forced mate or an incoming tactic that demanded direct action. The tagger tags fire only on scattered side-effects (allowed mate, allowed battery, missed overloading) that differ per position and never name the shared 'tempo-losing move that ignores an urgent threat' concept, which the ALT label captures precisely.

Every position shares the same error: playing a slow, non-forcing move (often a pawn push) when a forcing sequence — a mate, a check-driven combination, or a winning capture — was available. The ALT label 'Slow Move Missing Tactic' pinpoints this shared thread better than the fragmented tactic-specific tags.

In nearly every position the winning line is a forcing check or sacrifice (Rxh3+, Re1+, Bxf2+, Bxh2+, Nc5+) that DEFLECTS a defender to win the opponent's queen, while the player instead made a slow/quiet move. The tagger offers related generics like 'Missed Attacking Check' and 'Missed Overloading' but never names the specific deflection-sacrifice-wins-queen motif. The ALT label 'Slow Move Missing Tactic' captures the shared quiet-move-misses-forcing-shot pattern more faithfully than any single tag.

Across the positions the shared mistake is playing a forcing-looking check that either hangs material (Qxb4+, Qg5+, Qe8+) or simply accomplishes nothing while throwing away the win (Ra1+, Rg8+, Re8+). The tagger's 'Pointless Check' tag (and 'Hung Queen' for the queen-hanging subset) directly names this core concept. The ALT label only captures the queen-hanging cases and misses the several pointless-but-non-hanging checks, so it is narrower.

Most top positions share the same mistake: the player failed to capture White's/Black's undefended queen (Bxf3, axb4, Bxc3, Nxd2) or left their own queen en prise. The ALT label is essentially equivalent (generic hanging piece) and no more specific than the family.
opus_label: Missed Free Capture Of Hanging Piece

Every position shows White/Black greedily capturing (often a queen or rook) but thereby removing the only defender of the first/eighth rank, allowing a forced back-rank mate. The tag 'Allowed Back-Rank Mate' names this specific concept precisely, so it is covered.

Across positions the shared mistake is leaving a major piece—usually the queen—en prise, whether by moving it into a line of fire (2,6), failing to defend it (4,7), removing its own defender (1), or capturing a defended piece and losing the recapture (5,8). Every position is a voluntary capture/exchange that liquidates into a lost king-and-pawn (or minor-piece) endgame, removing the defender's last dynamic piece. The ALT label 'Wasted Tempo Blunder' inverts the concept (these miss a gaining push rather than waste one), so it is less accurate.

The positions share a king move or pawn push that strips away shelter and walks the king into a barrage of checks (perpetual in [1][2][8], forced mate in [4]). Most top positions ([1][2][3][5][6]) involve placing or leaving a piece on an undefended square where it is immediately captured, the essence of hanging material. The tagger's 'Hung Material' and 'Allowed Hanging Piece' families directly name this concept. The ALT label 'Leaving Piece Hanging' says the same thing but is not more specific than the covering tag.

In nearly every position Black/White missed a knight move (Ne3+, Nd2+, Nd4+, Nc6, Nd3) that forks the king and rook, winning material outright. The tagger's top tag 'Missed Knight Fork' names this precisely, and the 'Missed Fork' family also covers it. The ALT label is identical, so it offers no improvement.

The positions all share dropping/losing a minor piece (or pawn) in the opening—e.g. Nxe5 losing to the c6 recapture, the c5 bishop left hanging to bxc5/dxc5, or h6 failing to address exd4. The ALT label 'King Walked Into Mate' is a narrower framing that fits some but not all cases (several are removing a defender rather than the king moving), so it isn't clearly better.

Most top positions involve failing to grab an undefended enemy piece — the free bishop on b7/g7, a free knight, or a desperado rook that should capture before being lost. The positions revolve around loose, undefended pieces: several miss free captures (Qxd4, Qxg4, ignoring attacked knights) while others push or capture into losing their own material. Every position is a missed free capture of an undefended enemy piece (rook in most, queen in [4][5]), where the player moved elsewhere and left the winning capture on the board. The tagger's 'Missed Free Rook'/'Missed Free Queen' tags and the 'Missed Free Material' family name this exactly. The ALT label is equivalent but not more precise than the specific tags.

Most top positions (2,3,4,5,7,8) are blunders that abandon the first/eighth rank and permit a forced back-rank mate via a rook or queen invasion. The tagger's 'Allowed Back-Rank Mate' tag names this specific concept directly, so it is covered.
